\section[\ar{الظهر} \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل}]{\ar{الظهر}, \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل} — noon and midnight}

\label{lesson:AR-C15-ad-duhr-muntasaf-al-layl}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Noon in Arabic isn't just a clock-time word — it's tied directly into the rhythm of daily prayer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{الظهر} — noon, and a prayer}
\textbf{\ar{الظهر}} (\emph{aẓ-ẓuhr} or \emph{adh-dhuhr}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{noon}\textquotedblright{} — from the root \textbf{\ar{ظ}-\ar{ه}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ẓ-h-r}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to appear, become visible}\textquotedblright{} (the sun standing at its highest, most visible point). Be honest about what makes this word different from Spanish's \emph{mediodía}: \textbf{\ar{الظهر} is also the name of the midday Islamic prayer}, \emph{ṣalāt al-ẓuhr}. For a Muslim, \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}time for the noon prayer\textquotedblright{} are the same word — this isn't a neutral clock-time term the way \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} or \emph{mediodía} are in cultures where the day isn't organized around five fixed prayer times.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل} — a transparent \textquotedblleft{}half of the night\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ar{منتصف} \ar{الليل}} (\emph{muntaṣaf al-layl}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{midnight},\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the half of the night}.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\ar{منتصف}} (\emph{muntaṣaf}) comes from the root \textbf{\ar{ن}-\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}} (\emph{n-ṣ-f}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{half}\textquotedblright{} (the same root as \textbf{\ar{نصف}}, \emph{niṣf}, \textquotedblleft{}a half\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{\ar{الليل}} (\emph{al-layl}) is simply \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the night}.\textquotedblright{} This one is fully transparent — no erosion, no double meaning, just \textquotedblleft{}the middle of the night,\textquotedblright{} structurally exactly like Latin's \emph{media nox}.

(\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{The half of the night}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{muntaṣaf}, from \textbf{\ar{ن}-\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}} \emph{n-ṣ-f}, \textquotedblleft{}half.\textquotedblright{}) Is Arabic's word for noon a neutral clock-time word the way Spanish's \emph{mediodía} is? (\textbf{No} — it's bound up with the daily prayer schedule.)
